title: Why Amazon KDP Keeps Rejecting My PDF
description: Amazon KDP keeps rejecting your PDF? Learn the most common manuscript and cover PDF rejection causes, how to diagnose them, and how to fix trim size, bleed, safe area, resolution, fonts, transparency, barcode, and file validation errors.
metaTitle: Amazon KDP Keeps Rejecting My PDF: Complete Fix Guide
metaDescription: Fix repeated KDP PDF rejections with this complete guide to trim size, bleed, safe area, cover mismatch, low resolution, fonts, transparency, barcode errors, and oversized PDFs.
ogTitle: Why Amazon KDP Keeps Rejecting My PDF

excerpt: If Amazon KDP keeps rejecting your PDF even though it opens normally in Canva or Acrobat, the problem is usually hidden print-validation data. This guide shows you how to diagnose and fix the most common KDP PDF rejection causes.
keywords: Amazon KDP keeps rejecting my PDF

shortAnswer: Amazon KDP usually keeps rejecting a PDF because the file is not print-ready even though it opens normally. The most common causes are wrong trim size, incorrect bleed, safe-area violations, cover and interior mismatches, low-resolution images, missing embedded fonts, complex transparency, oversized files, barcode conflicts, or corrupted PDF exports.

faqs.question: Why does Amazon KDP keep rejecting my PDF?
faqs.answer: KDP keeps rejecting a PDF when the file fails print validation, not simply because it cannot open. A PDF can open normally in Canva, Preview, or Acrobat while still having the wrong trim size, missing bleed, unsafe text placement, low-resolution images, unembedded fonts, complex transparency, a barcode conflict, or corrupted export data. The fix is to diagnose the file as a print-production PDF, not only as a viewable document.

faqs.question: Why does my PDF look fine but KDP rejects it?
faqs.answer: Most PDF viewers only show whether the file can be displayed. KDP checks whether the file can be printed, trimmed, bound, and previewed correctly. That means it compares page dimensions, bleed, margins, cover size, spine width, font embedding, image quality, and processing complexity. A design can look perfect on screen while still failing a hidden KDP requirement.

faqs.question: What is the fastest way to find the cause of a KDP PDF rejection?
faqs.answer: Start with dimensions. Check the trim size selected in KDP, then check the exported PDF page size. After that, check bleed, safe area, image resolution, font embedding, transparency, file size, and barcode placement. If the rejection happens during preview generation, also test a clean browser and consider split-testing the manuscript to locate a problem page.

faqs.question: Can Canva PDFs be rejected by KDP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Canva can create usable KDP PDFs, but it can also produce files with wrong dimensions, missing bleed, oversized images, transparency-heavy pages, or elements too close to the edge. Exporting as PDF Print is important, but it does not automatically fix trim size, safe area, gutter, or cover wrap dimensions. Always inspect the exported PDF before upload.

faqs.question: Does KDP reject PDFs for low-resolution images?
faqs.answer: KDP can flag low-resolution images when images are too small for their printed size or have been stretched beyond usable quality. Aim for roughly 300 DPI at final print size for important raster images. Be careful with screenshots, AI-upscaled images, and Canva assets stretched across a full page or cover. A large file is not always high resolution; it may just be inefficient.

faqs.question: How do I know if fonts are embedded in my PDF?
faqs.answer: In Adobe Acrobat, open the PDF properties and check the Fonts tab. Fonts should show as embedded or embedded subset. If a font is missing, substituted, or restricted from embedding, KDP may render text incorrectly or reject the file. Re-export from the source app with font embedding enabled, use a different licensed font, or carefully outline text when appropriate.

faqs.question: Can a large PDF cause KDP upload rejection?
faqs.answer: Yes. Oversized PDFs are more likely to upload slowly, fail validation, freeze KDP Previewer, or time out during processing. This is common with coloring books, photo books, and Canva interiors made from huge PNG pages. Optimize images before export, flatten finished pages, avoid unnecessary transparency, and keep the file print-ready rather than bloated.

faqs.question: What does cover and interior do not match mean on KDP?
faqs.answer: It means the cover PDF and manuscript settings disagree. Common causes include different trim sizes, a cover built for an old page count, wrong paper type, wrong bleed assumption, or incorrect spine width. Because spine width depends on page count and paper type, even a small manuscript change can make a previously correct cover fail validation.

faqs.question: Should I compress my PDF before uploading to KDP?
faqs.answer: Compression can help if the PDF is unnecessarily heavy, but aggressive compression can blur images, damage line art, or rasterize text poorly. The safer workflow is to optimize source images at the correct final print size, flatten complex effects, export a clean print PDF, then use controlled PDF optimization only if needed. Do not blindly choose the smallest compressed file.

faqs.question: Can KDP reject a corrupted PDF even if Acrobat opens it?
faqs.answer: Yes. A PDF can open locally but still contain damaged fonts, malformed page boxes, broken image data, unsupported transparency, or artifacts from repeated conversions. KDP's rendering system may fail later during validation or preview generation. Re-export from the original source file, avoid converter chains, and upload a fresh PDF with a new filename.

summary: KDP PDF rejection usually means the file failed print validation, not that the PDF cannot open.
The most common causes are trim size, bleed, safe area, cover mismatch, low resolution, fonts, transparency, barcode placement, oversized files, and corrupted exports.
A systematic check is faster than repeated uploads: dimensions first, then bleed, safe area, resolution, fonts, layers, file size, and final re-export.
checklist: KDP trim size matches the source document.
Exported PDF dimensions match the selected trim and bleed setting.
Interior and cover use the same trim size.
Cover spine width matches final page count and paper type.
Bleed is enabled only when the PDF actually includes bleed.
Background art extends past trim when bleed is required.
Text, page numbers, borders, and logos stay inside safe areas.
Barcode area is clear of text, QR codes, logos, and important graphics.
Important images are close to 300 DPI at final print size.
Fonts are embedded or safely outlined.
Complex transparency and hidden layers are flattened or removed.
PDF file size is reasonable for the book type.
The PDF was exported from the original source file, not repeatedly converted.
The final PDF opens and page dimensions are checked in a PDF viewer.
The corrected file is preflighted before re-uploading to KDP.

steps.name: Check trim size and PDF dimensions
steps.text: Confirm the trim size selected in KDP matches the source file and the exported PDF page size.

steps.name: Verify bleed and safe area
steps.text: Make sure bleed is present only when required, background art extends outward, and important content stays inside the safe area.

steps.text: Check trim size, page count, paper type, spine width, and full cover wrap dimensions against the final manuscript.

content: You upload your manuscript to Amazon KDP. It rejects the PDF. You fix something small, export again, upload again, and KDP rejects it again. The PDF opens perfectly on your computer. Canva says the design is fine. Adobe Acrobat does not show an obvious problem. Yet Amazon KDP still refuses the file.

That loop is maddening because KDP often gives you a short warning instead of a complete diagnosis. The real problem is usually hidden inside the production details of the PDF: page boxes, trim size, bleed, fonts, image resolution, transparency, barcode space, or cover dimensions.

A PDF that opens is not automatically a print-ready PDF. KDP has to print it, trim it, bind it, generate a browser preview, and sometimes send it through manual review. This guide shows you how to diagnose the rejection systematically instead of uploading the same broken file over and over.
## Quick Answer
Amazon KDP keeps rejecting your PDF because the file fails one or more print-readiness checks. The most common causes are:
- Wrong trim size.
- Missing or incorrect bleed.
- Text, page numbers, borders, or logos outside the safe area.
- Low-resolution images.
- Cover size mismatch.
- Fonts not embedded.
- Complex transparency or hidden layers.
- Corrupted PDF export.
- Oversized PDF file.
- Cover and interior mismatch.
If you are stuck right now, check dimensions first. A wrong trim size or wrong PDF page size makes every other measurement unreliable.
## How Amazon KDP Actually Reviews PDFs

KDP does not review your PDF like a normal PDF viewer. A desktop viewer mainly asks, "Can this file be opened and displayed?" KDP asks, "Can this file be manufactured as a paperback or hardcover without production problems?"

The process usually includes several layers. First, KDP receives the upload and checks whether the file is readable. Then it performs automated validation on dimensions, page count, bleed, fonts, images, and file structure. Next, it generates Previewer output so you can inspect the book. After that, the file still needs to pass print-readiness checks and may be reviewed manually.
This is why successful upload does not equal approved file. A PDF can upload successfully and still fail later when KDP tries to render the proof or compare the cover with the interior.

KDP's official help pages are useful references while troubleshooting, especially the [print book formatting guidelines](https://kdp.amazon.com/help/topic/G201857950), [cover formatting guidance](https://kdp.amazon.com/help/topic/G201834180), and [cover calculator/templates](https://kdp.amazon.com/cover-calculator).
## PDF Rejection Category Overview
| Category | Typical error | Severity | Difficulty to fix |
| Size | PDF dimensions do not match trim | High | Medium |
| Bleed | Artwork reaches edge without bleed | High | Medium |
| Safe area | Text or page numbers too close to trim | High | Easy to medium |
| Resolution | Images below print quality | Medium to high | Medium |
| Fonts | Fonts missing or not embedded | High | Easy to medium |
| Cover | Cover/interior mismatch | High | Medium to hard |
| Spine | Spine width built for wrong page count | High | Medium |
| Barcode | Text or graphics in barcode area | High | Easy |
| Transparency | Live effects or hidden layers fail rendering | Medium | Medium |
| Corruption | PDF opens locally but fails KDP rendering | High | Medium |

The point of this table is not to guess. It is to choose an order. Start with size and bleed because they affect the whole file. Then inspect content placement, images, fonts, layers, file size, and corruption.
## Reason #1: Wrong Trim Size
Wrong trim size is one of the fastest ways to create a KDP PDF rejection. It happens when the book setup in KDP says one physical size, but your PDF was designed or exported at another size.

For example, your Canva file might be 8.5 x 11 inches while KDP is set to 6 x 9. Or your manuscript might be built as a no-bleed 6 x 9 PDF while the KDP upload expects a bleed-sized file. The file may look centered in a viewer, but KDP is comparing it against the trim size you selected.

How to identify it: open the exported PDF properties and check the page size. Then compare that number with the trim size in KDP and the document setup in your source app. Do this for both manuscript and cover.

How to fix it: change the source document to the correct trim size and reflow the layout. Avoid simply scaling the finished PDF unless you understand how scaling affects margins, image resolution, and safe area. Scaling can make text too close to the edge or reduce image quality.
If the problem is a cover template mismatch, use [KDP Cover Dimensions Not Matching Template](/blog/kdp-cover-dimensions-not-matching-template) before rebuilding the cover.
## Reason #2: Wrong Bleed Setup

Bleed is extra artwork that extends beyond the final trim edge. It is trimmed off during production. You need bleed when photos, backgrounds, color blocks, illustrations, or patterns are supposed to reach the physical edge of the page.

A wrong bleed setup can happen two ways. First, the design needs bleed but the PDF was exported at trim size. Second, KDP is set to bleed but the PDF does not include the expected extra page dimensions or extended artwork.

Coloring books, puzzle books, activity books, children's books, comics, and photo books often trigger bleed confusion because they use full-page art or borders. If line art touches the edge, it needs correct bleed. If a puzzle grid is intended to stay inside white margins, it should not sit near trim.
How to identify it: look at whether any printed content reaches the page edge. Then compare the PDF page size against KDP's expected size for bleed or no bleed.

How to fix it: extend expendable background artwork outward into bleed and keep important content inward. Do not put text, page numbers, puzzle clues, or logos in the bleed area. For the decision framework, see [KDP Bleed vs No Bleed](/blog/kdp-bleed-vs-no-bleed).
## Reason #3: Text Outside Safe Area

Safe area problems happen when important content sits too close to trim, fold, barcode area, or gutter. KDP may describe this as text outside safe area, margin too small, or content too close to the edge.

On covers, common offenders include subtitles, author names, award badges, QR codes, logos, and decorative borders. On interiors, common offenders include page numbers, headers, footers, puzzle grids, captions, and line art.

A border can fail even if it is not text. KDP sees it as printable content near trim. A footer page number can fail even when body text is fine. A hidden template mark near the edge can fail even when the visible page looks clean.
How to identify it: inspect the warning page in KDP Previewer, then open the exported PDF at 100% zoom. Check every edge, especially the bottom edge and binding side.

How to fix it: move important content inward, raise low page numbers, widen margins, and remove hidden objects. For a focused walkthrough, use [KDP Margin Too Small Error](/blog/fix-kdp-margin-too-small-error) and [KDP Safe Area Explained](/blog/kdp-safe-area-explained).
## Reason #4: Cover and Interior Do Not Match
KDP compares the cover and interior together. A cover PDF is not just a front image; it is a full production wrap that depends on trim size, paper type, page count, spine width, and bleed.

A common example: you designed a paperback cover when the manuscript had 120 pages. Later, formatting changes increased the manuscript to 148 pages. The spine width is now different, but the cover PDF still uses the old spine. KDP rejects the cover because the wrap no longer matches the final book.

Other mismatch causes include selecting cream paper in KDP while the cover was calculated for white paper, changing trim size after designing the cover, uploading a front-cover-only PDF as a full cover, or mixing bleed and no-bleed assumptions.
How to identify it: compare the interior trim, final page count, paper type, bleed setting, and cover template dimensions. If any one of these changed, rebuild the cover from the latest values.

How to fix it: finalize the manuscript first, then calculate or download the correct cover template. Rebuild the full cover wrap. For spine-specific fixes, see [KDP Spine Width Wrong](/blog/kdp-spine-width-wrong).
## Reason #5: Low Resolution Images

KDP can reject or warn about PDFs when important images are too low resolution for their printed size. This is common with screenshots, stretched Canva images, AI art enlarged beyond its real detail, and rasterized text.

Print quality is usually measured in DPI: dots or pixels per inch at final print size. A small 900-pixel image might be acceptable as a small icon but poor as a full-page illustration. Upscaling can increase pixel count without adding real detail, so the image may still look soft in print.

How to verify image quality: check the original image pixel dimensions and divide by the printed size in inches. A full 6 x 9 page at 300 DPI needs roughly 1800 x 2700 pixels before bleed. A full 8.5 x 11 page needs roughly 2550 x 3300 pixels.

How to fix it: replace low-resolution images with higher-quality originals, avoid screenshots, export line art cleanly, and do not stretch small assets. For a deeper image workflow, see [How to Fix Low Resolution Images Errors on Amazon KDP](/blog/fix-low-resolution-images-kdp).
## Reason #6: Fonts Are Not Embedded
Font embedding means the PDF carries the font data needed to render the text correctly. If fonts are not embedded, KDP may substitute them, render text incorrectly, or reject the file.
This matters because your computer may have the font installed while KDP's processing system does not. The PDF can look fine on your machine but behave differently when Amazon renders it.
How to identify it: open the PDF in Adobe Acrobat, check File Properties, then inspect the Fonts tab. Fonts should say embedded or embedded subset. If they do not, the PDF is risky.

How to fix it: export from the source app with font embedding enabled. Use fonts that allow embedding. If a font cannot be embedded, switch to a licensed alternative or outline display text carefully. Do not outline long body text unless you understand the file-size and accessibility tradeoffs.
## Reason #7: Transparency and Hidden Layers

Transparency, blend modes, masks, shadows, and hidden layers can make a PDF harder for KDP to process. This is especially common in Canva, Illustrator, Photoshop, Affinity, and InDesign files that contain stacked effects.

The problem is not that transparency is always forbidden. The problem is that complex live effects can fail during KDP rasterization or create huge files. Hidden template layers or old objects near the edge can also trigger rejection.
How to identify it: inspect the source file layers. Look for transparent PNGs, shadows, glows, blend modes, masks, locked template layers, and old objects outside the artboard or page.

How to fix it: keep an editable master file, then create a flattened upload copy. Flatten finished effects, remove hidden objects, delete template marks, and export a clean print PDF. For Previewer freezes caused by processing complexity, read [KDP Previewer Not Loading](/blog/kdp-previewer-not-loading).
## Reason #8: Oversized PDF Files

Oversized PDFs are not always rejected immediately, but they often cause upload failures, validation delays, Previewer freezes, or timeouts. This is common with coloring books, photo books, mosaic books, and Canva interiors built from huge PNG pages.

A PDF can be huge for good reasons, such as a long full-color photo book. But many KDP PDFs are huge for bad reasons: images far larger than the final print size, repeated full-page PNGs, live transparency, duplicate assets, or repeated PDF conversions.

How to identify it: check file size and inspect the largest source assets. If the file is hundreds of megabytes and the book is not a complex photo book, look for oversized images or unflattened pages.

How to fix it: resize images to about 300 DPI at final print size, flatten finished pages, avoid unnecessary transparent PNGs, export once from the source file, and use controlled PDF optimization only when needed.
## Reason #9: Barcode Area Contains Text

For printed books, KDP needs a clear barcode area on the back cover unless you provide a compliant barcode workflow. If text, QR codes, logos, borders, or important graphics sit in that reserved zone, KDP can reject the cover.

This often happens when creators place a website URL, logo, decorative frame, or author bio too low on the back cover. A subtle background texture is usually less risky than readable content or high-contrast graphics.
How to identify it: use the official KDP cover template and inspect the lower-right back cover. Anything important inside the barcode box should move.

How to fix it: redesign the back cover with the barcode zone as a reserved production area. Keep blurbs, logos, QR codes, and decorative borders away from it. The focused fix is here: [How to Fix Barcode Area Contains Text on KDP](/blog/fix-barcode-area-contains-text-kdp).
## Reason #10: Corrupted PDF Files
A corrupted PDF can still open. That is what makes this category so confusing. Acrobat may display the pages, but KDP may fail later during validation, rendering, or print conversion.

Common causes include incomplete exports, damaged embedded fonts, repeated PDF compression, converter chains, unsupported effects, malformed page boxes, or image data that renders locally but fails in KDP's pipeline.
Symptoms include vague upload failure, Previewer freezing on the same file, errors that disappear after a fresh export, or one page repeatedly breaking the manuscript.

How to fix it: return to the original source file, export a fresh print PDF, avoid web converter chains, give the file a new name, and upload the clean export. If a single page is suspicious, split-test the manuscript to isolate it.
## The Complete Troubleshooting Workflow
Use this order when KDP rejects a PDF repeatedly:
1. PDF rejected.
2. Check trim size.
3. Check exported PDF dimensions.
4. Check bleed setting and bleed artwork.
5. Check safe area, margins, and gutter.
6. Check image resolution.
7. Check embedded fonts.
8. Check transparency, hidden layers, and template marks.
9. Check file size and processing complexity.
10. Check barcode zone and cover/interior match.
11. Re-export a fresh print PDF.
12. Upload again.
This order prevents wasted work. If the trim size is wrong, do not spend an hour optimizing images first. If the cover template is wrong, compression will not fix it.
## Coloring Book Specific Rejections
Coloring books are rejection-prone because they combine edge-sensitive artwork, repeated pages, borders, and large image assets.

Borders near trim are a classic problem. They can trigger safe-area warnings and also look uneven after printing. Full-page black backgrounds need bleed. Dot books and mosaic books often include tiny numbers near edges. Color-by-number books may include small labels that become unsafe when pages are scaled.

For coloring books, check every repeated template. If one page border is too close to trim, the same mistake may appear across the entire manuscript. Fix the master layout, not just one exported page.

Also check file weight. A 120-page coloring book made from oversized transparent PNGs can become huge without improving print quality. Flatten line art onto white pages when transparency is not needed.
## Canva Users: Most Common PDF Mistakes
Canva is popular for KDP, but KDP does not know that your file came from Canva. It only sees the exported PDF.

Common Canva mistakes include using the wrong custom dimensions, exporting Standard PDF instead of PDF Print, forgetting bleed, placing page numbers too low, using a front-cover-only canvas for a full paperback wrap, stretching small images, leaving template marks visible, and stacking transparency-heavy elements across many pages.

The fix is to set the document size before designing, use guides, lock the KDP template when designing covers, keep important content inside safe areas, export as PDF Print, and inspect the exported PDF properties before upload.
For export-specific setup, use [Canva to KDP Export Settings](/blog/canva-to-kdp-export-settings).
## How KDPPreflight Helps

KDPPreflight helps by checking the final PDF before you give it to Amazon. It is not a promise of approval because KDP is the final validator and requirements can change. But it gives you a practical preflight pass that catches the issues most likely to create rejection loops.

It can help validate trim size, manuscript and cover dimensions, bleed setup, safe-area risks, spine width, resolution, and general PDF readiness. That is useful because KDP's rejection message often names the symptom but not the full cause.
Use KDPPreflight after exporting the final PDF, not only while designing. The exported PDF is the file KDP will analyze.
## Preventing Future Rejections
Use this 15-point checklist before every upload:
- Finalize manuscript page count before designing the cover.
- Confirm trim size before building the document.
- Use the correct KDP cover template.
- Match cover, interior, paper type, and page count.
- Check PDF dimensions after export.
- Choose bleed only when the file includes bleed.
- Extend backgrounds into bleed when needed.
- Keep text and page numbers inside safe areas.
- Keep barcode area clear.
- Use images around 300 DPI at final print size.
- Embed fonts.
- Flatten complex transparency in the upload copy.
- Remove hidden objects and template marks.
- Avoid repeated PDF conversion chains.
- Run a preflight check before uploading.
## Conclusion

Most KDP PDF rejections are technical. That is good news, because technical problems can be diagnosed. The file may look fine in Canva or Acrobat, but KDP is checking whether it can become a printed book.

Do not keep uploading the same file and hoping the warning changes. Work through the production checks in order: trim size, PDF dimensions, bleed, safe area, cover/interior match, resolution, fonts, transparency, file size, barcode, and corruption.

A systematic validation process turns repeated rejection into a fixable checklist. Before the next upload, run your final PDF through [KDPPreflight](/tools/kdp-cover-checker) so you can catch the most common print-readiness problems before Amazon KDP does.
